elements.id-string-3: The large-scale visual pretraining has significantly improve the performance of large vision models.
elements.id-string-4: However, we observe the \emph{low FLOPs pitfall} that the existing low-FLOPs models cannot benefit from large-scale pretraining.In this paper, we propose a general design principle of adding more parameters while maintaining low FLOPs for large-scale visual pretraining, named as ParameterNet.
elements.id-string-5: Dynamic convolutions are used for instance to equip the networks with more parameters and only slightly increase the FLOPs.
elements.id-string-6: The proposed ParameterNet scheme enables low-FLOPs networks to benefit from large-scale visual pretraining.
elements.id-string-7: Experiments on the large-scale ImageNet-22K have shown the superiority of our ParameterNet scheme.
elements.id-string-8: For example, ParameterNet-600M can achieve higher accuracy than the widely-used Swin Transformer (81.6\% \emph{vs.} 80.9\%) and has much lower FLOPs (0.6G \emph{vs.} 4.5G).

elements.id-string-11: Thanks to the development of computation hardware and data engineering, the large-scale visual pretraining as a fundamental component in computer vision has made impressive progress.
elements.id-string-12: The pretrained vision models serve as the representation learners and transfer to downstream tasks such as image recognition~\cite{vit,efficientnetv2} and object detection~\cite{swin}.
elements.id-string-13: The mainstream pretrained vision models usually requires a large amount of resources including data, parameters and FLOPs.
elements.id-string-14: These three key factors heavily influence the performance and basically follow the scaling law~\cite{zhai2022scaling}.
elements.id-string-15: The large pretraining data can provide diverse samples for representation learning.
elements.id-string-16: The sizes of these datasets range from millions~\cite{imagenet,kuznetsova2020open} to billions~\cite{sun2017revisiting,thomee2015new}, for example, the widely-used ImageNet-22K dataset~\cite{imagenet} consists of 14M images and 21,841 categories.
elements.id-string-17: To better fitting on the large dataset, the model sizes (including both parameters and FLOPs) are getting larger and larger in recent years, \eg, ViT-G/14 model has 1.8B parameters and 965B FLOPs~\cite{zhai2022scaling}.
elements.id-string-18: The visual applications on mobile devices usually requires fast inference, so it is difficult to deploy the existing pretrained vision models due to the high computational cost.
elements.id-string-19: To address this issue, we empirically study the effect of FLOPs in large-scale visual pretraining.
elements.id-string-20: ImageNet-22K is adopted as the large-scale pretraining data and ImageNet-1K is a relatively small dataset for comparison.
elements.id-string-21: The pretrained transformer and CNN models are then finetuned on ImageNet-1K to evaluate the performance.
elements.id-string-22: As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:swin} and \ref{fig:enetv2}, when model FLOPs gradually increase, the model accuracy increases consistently.
elements.id-string-23: For the high-FLOPs models, 22K pretrained models outperform 1K ones.
elements.id-string-24: However, the low-FLOPs models cannot benifit from large-scale pretraining, and we called this observation as \emph{low FLOPs pitfall}.
elements.id-string-25: In this paper, we construct low-FLOPs ParameterNet by adding more parameters while maintaining low FLOPs for large-scale visual pretraining.
elements.id-string-26: It is a general design principle and there are various approaches with more parameters and low FLOPs.
elements.id-string-27: For instance, here we mainly consider the efficient dynamic convolution which manyfold increase the number of parameters while almost does not bring in extra FLOPs.
elements.id-string-28: The ParameterNet scheme can enable the previous networks to benefit from the large-scale visual pretraining and overcome the \emph{low FLOPs pitfall}.
elements.id-string-29: In the experiments, the ImageNet-22K pretrained ParameterNets can improve the performance by about +2\% over the regular ImageNet-1K training.
elements.id-string-30: For example, ParameterNet-600M achieves 81.6\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K val set whose \#FLOPs is 7$\times$ lower than that of Swin-T.

elements.id-string-34: The deep neural networks in computer vision can be divided into CNNs, vision transformers and others.
elements.id-string-35: CNN used to be the mainstream network architecture for visual tasks~\cite{lecun1998gradient,alexnet,resnet}.
elements.id-string-36: The first trainable CNN \ie, LeNet~\cite{lecun1998gradient} is applied on optimal character recognition (a typical visual task).
elements.id-string-37: From 2012, CNNs began to be deeper and larger for more complex visual tasks, such as image classification~\cite{alexnet}, object detection~\cite{fasterRCNN} and semantic segmentation~\cite{fcn}.
elements.id-string-38: ResNet~\cite{resnet} introduces the shortcut connection to train the deeper networks and is widely used in vision and other communities.
elements.id-string-39: MobileNet~\cite{mobilenet} is designed for mobile devices and EfficientNet~\cite{efficientnet} scales the network from small to large.
elements.id-string-40: Vision transformer is introduced into visual tasks from 2020~\cite{vit-survey,vit,detr}.
elements.id-string-41: ViT~\cite{vit} is the first transformer backbone by dividing the image into patches and processing them using the standard transformer architcture.
elements.id-string-42: Then a number of variants and improvements are proposed incluidng the pyramid architectures~\cite{pvt,swin}, the local attentions~\cite{tnt,swin} and hybrid networks~\cite{guo2022cmt,metaformer}.
elements.id-string-43: Beyond CNNs and transformers, other types of neural networks are also explored for visual tasks.
elements.id-string-44: MLP-like architectures~\cite{mixer,resmlp} with only fully-connected layers as main operators can potentially simplify the software and hardware design for AI.
elements.id-string-45: The improved versions of MLP~\cite{cyclemlp,asmlp,hire,wavemlp} can enhance locality and translation equivalence.
elements.id-string-46: GNN has also been expored in vision and achieves competitive performance to transformers~\cite{vig}.
elements.id-string-48: Large-scale pretraining has achieved great success on natural language processing such as GPT series~\cite{gpt3,gpt4}.
elements.id-string-49: In the field of computer vision, large-scale pretraining is also beneficial and helps for downstream tasks~\cite{bit,swin,sam}.
elements.id-string-50: The large datasets are the foundations of pretraining.
elements.id-string-51: To distinguish from the regular ImageNet-1K training, we consider the dataset with an order of magnitude more than ImageNet-1K (\ie, more than 10M samples) as the large-scale dataset.
elements.id-string-52: The commonly-used large visual datasets include ImageNet-22K~\cite{imagenet}, JFT-300M~\cite{sun2017revisiting}, YFFCC100M~\cite{yfcc100m} and IG-1B-Targeted~\cite{yalniz2019billion}.
elements.id-string-53: The supervised pretraining is popular as it can learn semantic and meaningful representations for downstream visual tasks like segmentation and detection.
elements.id-string-54: BiT~\cite{bit} pretrained on JFT-300M achieves state-of-the-art on fine-grained recognition datasets.
elements.id-string-55: The ImageNet-22K pretrained Swin Transformer~\cite{swin} obtains high performance on segmentation and detection tasks.
elements.id-string-56: The unsupervised pretraining appeals many researchers as it does not requires labels and may leverage the massive unlabeled data.
elements.id-string-57: The most popular approaches of visual unsupervised pretraining are contrastive learning~\cite{he2020momentum,simclr} and masked image modeling (MIM)~\cite{bao2021beit,he2022masked,xie2022simmim}.
elements.id-string-58: In this paper, we utilize the vanilla supervised pretraining for simplicity and generality.
elements.id-string-60: The computational cost (\ie, FLOPs) is an important term in the scaling of visual models.
elements.id-string-61: We first investigate the effect of FLOPs and observe inspiring phenomenon.
elements.id-string-62: Both transformer and CNN architectures are studied on ImageNet-22K and ImageNet-1K pretraining.
elements.id-string-64: Swin Transformer~\cite{swin} is a representative vision transformer architecture with window attention and shifted window.
elements.id-string-65: We reproduce the models using the official code\footnote{https://github.com/microsoft/Swin-Transformer} and pretrain Swin Transformers with different scales on both ImageNet-22K and ImageNet-1K.
elements.id-string-66: The ImageNet-1k finetuning results are reported in Figure~\ref{fig:swin} for comparison.
elements.id-string-67: From the results, we can see that the accuracy increases as the FLOPs increase gradually with both ImageNet-1K and ImageNet-22K pretraining.
elements.id-string-68: For models with high FLOPs ($>$10G), pretraining on ImageNet-22K outperforms that on ImageNet-1K.
elements.id-string-69: However, pretraining on more data does not improve the performance for models with lower FLOPs ($<$4G).

elements.id-string-78: In this section, we investigate the low-FLOPs networks under large-scale pretraining setting.
elements.id-string-80: Here we do not propose a new architecture and select the most suitable low-FLOPs network architecture for large-scale visual pretraining.
elements.id-string-81: ViT~\cite{vit} and its variants~\cite{swin,tnt,pvt} have shown the superiority of transformer over CNN in the field of large vision models.
elements.id-string-82: As shown in Appendix~\ref{sec:paperswithcode}, Transformer-based models consistently outperform CNNs with similar computational cost when the FLOPs are higher than 5G FLOPs.
elements.id-string-83: As for smaller models especially mobile-level model within 600M FLOPs, CNN with inductive bias including locality and s translation equivariance remain dominant.
elements.id-string-84: To build efficient backbones for visual tasks, we select CNN as the base model.
elements.id-string-85: GhostNet~\cite{ghostnet} is the representative state-of-art mobile model which introduces cheap operation to simplify the standard convolutional layer.
elements.id-string-87: The number of parameters and FLOPs are highly corelated in neural networks.
elements.id-string-88: The model with large number of parameters usually has high FLOPs.
elements.id-string-89: Considering the intuition that large data requires more parameters, we construct ParameterNet by adding parameters while maintaining low FLOPs.
elements.id-string-90: We start from the conventional convolutional layer.
elements.id-string-91: Given the input feature $X\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{in}\times H\times W}$ and the weight tensor $W\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{out}\times C_{in}\times K\times K}$, the conventional convolutional layer operates as
elements.id-string-93: where $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{out}\times H'\times W'}$ is the output, $*$ is the convolution operation and the bias term is omitted for concision.
elements.id-string-94: The fully-connected layer can be viewed as the convolutional layer with $1\times1$ kernel size.
elements.id-string-95: Our design principle is adding more parameters while maintaining low FLOPs.
elements.id-string-96: There are various approaches to construct ParameterNet, such as dynamic convolution~\cite{dynamic-conv} and re-parameterized convolution~\cite{repvgg}.
elements.id-string-97: Although the re-parameterized convolution increase the number of parameters during training, its parameters and FLOPs are unchanged for inference, that is, the model capacity is not increased.
elements.id-string-98: In this paper, we mainly consider the efficient dynamic convolution which manyfold increase the number of parameters while almost does not bring in extra FLOPs.
elements.id-string-99: The dynamic convolution~\cite{dynamic-conv} with $M$ dynamic experts can be written as
elements.id-string-101: where $W_i\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{out}\times C_{in}\times H\times W}$ is the $i$-th convolutional weight tensor and $\alpha_i$ is the corresponding dynamic coefficient.
elements.id-string-102: The coefficient $\alpha_i$ is dynamically generated \wrt different input samples, and a typical manner is generating based on the input using MLP module.
elements.id-string-103: For the input $X$, a global average pooling is applied to fuse the information into a vector and then a two-layer MLP module with softmax activation is used to produce the coefficients dynamically:
elements.id-string-107: For the standard convolutional layer, the number of parameters is $C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K$ and the number of FLOPs are $H'\cdot W'\cdot C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K$.
elements.id-string-108: The dynamic convolution consists of coefficient generation module, dynamic weight fusion and convolution process.
elements.id-string-109: The coefficient generation module with $C_{in}$ hidden dimensions requires $C_{in}^2+C_{in}M$ parameters and $C_{in}^2+C_{in}M$ FLOPs.
elements.id-string-110: The dynamic weight fusion is parameter-free and has $M\cdot C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K$ FLOPs.
elements.id-string-111: Thus, the total numbers of parameters and FLOPs of dynamic convolution are $C_{in}^2+C_{in}M + M\cdot C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K$ and $C_{in}^2+C_{in}M + M\cdot C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K+H'\cdot W'\cdot C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K$ respectively.
elements.id-string-112: The parameter ratio of dynamic convolution over standard convolution is
elements.id-string-113: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} R_{param} &= \frac{C_{in}^2+C_{in}M + M\cdot C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K}{C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K} &= \frac{C_{in}}{C_{out}\cdot K\cdot K} + \frac{M}{C_{out}\cdot K\cdot K} + M &\approx \frac{1}{K^2} + M. \qquad (M<<C_{out}\cdot K\cdot K,~C_{in}\approx C_{out}) \end{aligned} \end{equation}
elements.id-string-115: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} R_{flops} &= \frac{C_{in}^2+C_{in}M + M\cdot C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K+H'\cdot W'\cdot C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K}{H'\cdot W'\cdot C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot K\cdot K} &= \frac{C_{in}}{H'\cdot W'\cdot C_{out}\cdot K\cdot K} + \frac{M}{H'\cdot W'\cdot C_{out}\cdot K\cdot K} + \frac{M}{H'\cdot W'} + 1 &\approx 1.  \qquad (1<M<<H'\cdot W',~C_{in}\approx C_{out}) \end{aligned} \end{equation}
elements.id-string-116: Thus, compared to the standard convolution, the dynamic convolution has about $M\times$ parameters with negligible extra FLOPs.

elements.id-string-222: However, we observe the \emph{low FLOPs pitfall} that the existing low-FLOPs models cannot benefit from large-scale pretraining.In this paper, we introduce a novel design principle, termed ParameterNet, aimed at augmenting the number of parameters in large-scale visual pretraining models while minimizing the increase in FLOPs.
elements.id-string-223: We leverage dynamic convolutions to incorporate additional parameters into the networks with only a marginal rise in FLOPs.
elements.id-string-224: The ParameterNet approach allows low-FLOPs networks to take advantage of large-scale visual pretraining.
elements.id-string-225: Furthermore, we extend the ParameterNet concept to the language domain to enhance inference results while preserving inference speed.Experiments on the large-scale ImageNet-22K have shown the superiority of our ParameterNet scheme.
elements.id-string-226: For example, ParameterNet-600M can achieve higher accuracy on ImageNet than the widely-used Swin Transformer (81.6\% \emph{vs.} 80.9\%) and has much lower FLOPs (0.6G \emph{vs.} 4.5G).

elements.id-string-229: Thanks to advancements in computational hardware and data engineering, large-scale visual pretraining has witnessed remarkable progress as a fundamental component in computer vision.
elements.id-string-230: Pretrained vision models act as efficient representation learners, showcasing their utility in various downstream visual tasks, including image recognition~\cite{imagenet,efficientnetv2}, object detection~\cite{swin,pvt} and semantic segmentation~\cite{he2017mask,setr}.
elements.id-string-231: The proposed ParameterNet can be extended to the large language model (LLM) domain and experiments on LLaMA model~\cite{llama} verify the effectiveness.
elements.id-string-234: The original GhostNet falls into the \emph{low FLOPs pitfall}.
elements.id-string-235: The proposed ParameterNet overcomes the \emph{low FLOPs pitfall}.}
elements.id-string-236: The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows.
elements.id-string-238: We observe an interesting phenomenon in large-scale visual pretraining called the \emph{low FLOPs pitfall}, that is, the performances of high-FLOPs models increase with more training data, but the models with low-FLOPs.We propose that parameters are more important than FLOPs for large-scale visual pretraining and further introduce the ParameterNet scheme by adding more parameters while maintaining low FLOPs.The proposed ParameterNet scheme can overcome the \emph{low FLOPs pitfall}, and experimental results on vision and language tasks show that ParameterNet achieves significantly higher performance with large-scale pretraining.

elements.id-string-265: Sparse-activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models~\cite{shazeer2017outrageously}, initially introduced in the NLP domain, allow for a substantial increase in the number of parameters while maintaining the computational load per token or sample unchanged.
elements.id-string-266: Numerous subsequent studies~\cite{zhou2022mixture,fedus2022switch,roller2021hash} have delved into exploring efficient routing mechanisms and have demonstrated the effectiveness of MoE in various large language models (LLMs) such as T5~\cite{t5}, NLLB~\cite{koishekenov2022memory}, LLaMA~\cite{llama} and Palm~\cite{palm}.
elements.id-string-267: In this context, our emphasis is primarily on low-FLOPs language models to validate the proposed hypothesis that incorporating more parameters can enhance the benefits of large-scale pretraining for low-FLOPs models, \ie, we proportionally reduce and construct a scaled-down version, LLaMA-1B.
elements.id-string-268: Much like MoE, our approach involves taking a token representation, denoted as $x$, and subsequently routing it to the top-$k$ determined experts from a set of $N$.
elements.id-string-269: The router module generates logits represented as $h(x) = softmax(router(x))$, creating a normalized distribution through a softmax function over the available $N$ experts at that particular layer.
elements.id-string-270: The top-$k$ experts, where we consistently set $k=1$ in our experiments to maintain similar FLOPs to the original counterparts, are then selected for routing the token $x$.
elements.id-string-271: The training loss on expert capacity (the number of tokens each expert computes) follows the setting in Switch Transformer~\cite{fedus2022switch}.
